theory.intro: A **compound event** joins two events with words such as *and*, *or*, *not*, *neither … nor*, *at least* and *at most*. Each phrase names a particular region of a Venn diagram, or a particular set of cells in a two-way table. Once you know which region the words describe, the probability is just the count in that region divided by the total number of outcomes — there is no need to add and subtract probabilities.
facts: '$A$ **and** $B$' is the overlap $A \cap B$; '$A$ **only**' is the part of $A$ outside $B$.
'$A$ **or** $B$, **or both**' (inclusive or) is every outcome in either circle, with the overlap counted **once**.
'$A$ **or** $B$, **but not both**' (exclusive or) is the same region with the overlap **removed**.
'**not** $A$' is everything outside circle $A$, which still includes the part of $B$ outside $A$.
'**neither** $A$ **nor** $B$' is only the region outside both circles.
'**at least** one' includes the boundary value, so at least one of two events means the same region as the inclusive or; '**more than** one' excludes it and means the overlap.
'**at most** one' means zero or one, so it is everything except the overlap.
Add the counts in the region, then divide by the total for the whole sample space and simplify. In a two-way table the total is the grand total in the bottom right corner.
The regions of a Venn diagram must add to the total, so a missing region can always be found by subtracting the others from the total.
steps: Fill in every region of the Venn diagram or table.
Identify the region the words describe.
Count that region and divide by the total, then simplify.

foundation.solution_text:
Both crescents are shaded but the overlap in the middle is not, so the shaded outcomes belong to exactly one of the two events.
The shaded region is '$A$ or $B$, but not both' — the exclusive or.
'$A$ or $B$, or both' would also shade the overlap, so it is the exclusive-or region together with $A \cap B$.

foundation.question_text:
The two-way table shows a survey of $50$ travellers.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Fiji} & \text{Not Fiji} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Bali} & 9 & 21 & 30 \\ \hline \text{Not Bali} & 6 & 14 & 20 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 15 & 35 & 50 \end{array}$
One traveller is chosen at random. Find the probability that they have visited Bali **and** Fiji, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
'And' needs both conditions, so read the single cell in the Bali row and the Fiji column.
That cell holds $9$ travellers, and the grand total is $50$.
$P(\text{Bali and Fiji}) = \frac{9}{50}$

development.question_text: In a survey of $36$ students, $20$ own a dog, $14$ own a cat and $6$ own both. Find the probability that a student chosen at random owns a dog or a cat, or both, as a fraction in simplest form.

In a survey of $45$ travellers, $28$ have visited Queensland, $19$ have visited Tasmania and $9$ have visited both. Find the probability that a traveller chosen at random has visited neither state, as a fraction in simplest form.

The two-way table shows a survey of $60$ students about pet ownership.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Cat} & \text{No cat} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Dog} & 11 & 19 & 30 \\ \hline \text{No dog} & 14 & 16 & 30 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 25 & 35 & 60 \end{array}$
One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that they own at most one of the two kinds of pet, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
'At most one' means zero or one pet, so every cell counts except the $11$ students who own both.
$60 - 11 = 49$
$P(\text{at most one}) = \frac{49}{60}$

development.question_text:
The two-way table shows a survey of $60$ students about pet ownership.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Cat} & \text{No cat} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Dog} & 11 & 19 & 30 \\ \hline \text{No dog} & 14 & 16 & 30 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 25 & 35 & 60 \end{array}$
One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that they do **not** own a cat, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
'Not a cat owner' is the whole 'No cat' column, which includes students who own a dog and students who own no pet at all.
$P(\text{no cat}) = \frac{19 + 16}{60}$
$= \frac{35}{60}$
$= \frac{7}{12}$

Everything outside circle $A$ is shaded, including the crescent of $B$ that lies outside $A$.
The shaded region is 'not $A$'.
'Neither $A$ nor $B$' would leave that crescent of $B$ unshaded, since those outcomes are still in $B$.
So 'not $A$' is the larger region: it is 'neither $A$ nor $B$' together with '$B$ only'.

development.question_text:
The two-way table shows a survey of $50$ travellers.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Fiji} & \text{Not Fiji} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Bali} & 9 & 21 & 30 \\ \hline \text{Not Bali} & 6 & 14 & 20 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 15 & 35 & 50 \end{array}$
One traveller is chosen at random. Find the probability that they have visited at least one of the two destinations, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
'At least one' covers every cell except the $14$ travellers who have visited neither destination.
$50 - 14 = 36$
$P(\text{at least one}) = \frac{36}{50}$
$= \frac{18}{25}$

mastery.question_text: In a survey of $50$ travellers, $32$ have visited Bali, $27$ have visited Fiji and $5$ have visited neither. Find the probability that a traveller chosen at random has visited Bali or Fiji, but not both, as a fraction in simplest form.

In a music school of $60$ students, $38$ play the piano, $29$ play the guitar and $11$ play neither instrument. Find the probability that a student chosen at random plays at most one of the two instruments, as a fraction in simplest form.

The two-way table shows a survey of $60$ households.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Cat} & \text{No cat} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Dog} & 12 & 23 & 35 \\ \hline \text{No dog} & 9 & 16 & 25 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 21 & 39 & 60 \end{array}$
One household is chosen at random. Find the probability that it does not own a dog, or owns a cat, or both, as a fraction in simplest form.
mastery.solution_text:
'Does not own a dog' is the whole 'No dog' row, and 'owns a cat' is the whole 'Cat' column.
The inclusive or takes every cell in either the row or the column, counting the shared cell once.
The 'No dog' row holds $9 + 16 = 25$ households.
The 'Cat' column adds the $12$ households that own a dog and a cat; the $9$ in the corner cell are already counted.
$P(\text{no dog, or cat, or both}) = \frac{25 + 12}{60}$
$= \frac{37}{60}$
